Early mobilisation and 90-day mortality in adults receiving mechanical ventilation
Smith J, Okafor A, Lindqvist P, et al. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID 38123456 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38123456/). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2400001 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2400001).

CLINICAL QUESTION (PICO)
  Population:   Adults in intensive care ventilated for at least 48 hours
  Intervention: Structured early mobilisation started within 72 hours of intubation
  Comparison:   Usual physiotherapy at the discretion of the treating team
  Outcome:      Death from any cause within 90 days

STUDY DESIGN
  Randomized controlled trial
  Parallel-group design
  Detected from publication type. Evidence: Randomized Controlled Trial (publication type), randomly assigned (abstract keyword).

KEY RESULTS
  CER (control event rate):      26.0%
  EER (experimental event rate): 16.0%
  ARR (absolute risk reduction): 10.0 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 16.5)
  RRR (relative risk reduction): 38.5%
  NNT 10 (95% CI 7–29)

  Appraised from: Abstract only.
  An Unclear verdict means the source above does not settle that question: it records a limit on what the reader could check, not a fault found in the study. Where an item was checked against a different document, that source is shown beside its verdict.

  Internal validity
    1. Was the allocation sequence generated using a genuinely random and unpredictable method?
       Verdict: Yes
    2. Was allocation concealed until each participant was irreversibly enrolled?
       Verdict: Unclear
    3. Were there no clinically important baseline imbalances that suggest a problem with the randomization process?
       Verdict: Yes
    4. Were deviations from the assigned interventions unlikely to bias the result, considering who knew the assigned treatment?
       Verdict: No
    5. Were outcome data sufficiently complete, with missingness unlikely to bias the estimated treatment effect?
       Verdict: Yes

       Verdict: Yes (source: Full text)
    7. Was the primary analysis appropriate for the treatment effect the trial intended to estimate, while preserving the randomized comparison as far as possible?
       Verdict: —
    8. Were the primary outcome and primary analysis prespecified, with no evidence that the reported result was selected from multiple outcomes, measurements, time points, or analyses?
       Verdict: No

  Applicability
    Applicability is not internal validity. A trial can be conducted impeccably and still not transfer to the patient in front of you, and a trial with real methodological weaknesses can still be about exactly your patient. Nothing below is a verdict on how the study was run.
    9. Are the participants, interventions, comparator, outcomes, and setting sufficiently similar to the clinical context in which the result would be used?
       Verdict: —

  Funding & conflicts
    Recorded as fact, never scored. Industry funding is not by itself a source of bias, and a field left blank means nothing was recorded here — not that there was nothing to record.

  Notes on flagged items
    Items answered No — judgements the reader made, about the study or about its fit:
      Item 4: Open label. Mortality is a hard endpoint, so this matters less here than it would for a symptom score.
      Item 8: (no note)
    Items answered Unclear — the source used does not settle these, which is not a finding against the study:
      Item 2: The abstract says "randomly assigned" and nothing about who held the sequence. Usually needs the full text — an abstract rarely has this detail.

BOTTOM LINE
  A 10 percentage point difference in 90-day mortality is large for this population, and the trial was stopped early at an interim look, so the estimate is probably optimistic. I would read the methods before taking the size of the effect at face value.
